rss.title: Rapidly scaling online storage to serve over 1 billion ChatGPT users (Part II)
rss.summary: Learn how OpenAI scaled Habitat with reliable multi-tenancy, global caching, and Azure Cosmos DB to deliver 12× faster reads for ChatGPT.
rss.text_excerpt:
All OpenAI products require fast, reliable access to data, provided by our storage platform, Habitat. It has to respond in milliseconds to over 1 billion users across 40 geographic regions. Our infrastructure faced an extraordinary challenge: supporting explosive growth and new use cases while continuing to improve reliability, performance, and product developer velocity. Solving that challenge required rethinking how our online storage platform was designed and operated. We constantly evaluated tradeoffs, following the pattern of: first become reliable enough for mission-critical product traffic, then fast enough for global users, and, finally, to deftly operate at massive scale. This two-part series explains how we developed Habitat from a simple client library and database into a globally distributed storage platform serving over 500 petabytes of data. Part I focused on Habitat’s evolution from a Python client to a service. It also covered the techniques that allowed us to push a Python-based service far beyond what many would consider practical. In this post, Part II, we walk through how we scaled the underlying storage component: Azure Cosmos DB. Through a close working partnership with the Azure team, we arrived at a viable multi-tenancy approach of co-managed containers, with excellent read performance at massive, global scale. Request Response Changes (CDC) As companies scale, infra teams often evolve from running single-tenant systems to multi-tenant ones. Single-tenancy, where every product surface team maintains their own system, reduces blast radius and provides easy ownership boundaries and workload isolation. As teams and product surfaces grow, this becomes expensive to run. Single-tenancy makes every product team responsible for capacity planning and often results in significant over-provisioning. Conversely, multi-tenancy assigns control to a centralized database team, with better knowledge and experience for provisioning resources. But multi-tenancy creates its own problems, such as noisy-neighbor issues, where one tenant consumes an unusually large share of the resources to the detriment of the other tenants. In Habitat, we had to weigh all these tradeoffs to design a reliable, efficient, storage system at scale. rss.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
rss.summary: AI models are solving more mathematical problems. A pattern is emerging in their successes that could help us predict which problems they’ll solve next.
rss.text_excerpt:
The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Problem complexity Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts: Look for a counterexample. Take the best known construction and generalize it. Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm. Gowers’ proposed formula for complexity is 2^k + t, where k is the length of the shortest hint sequence and t is the work required to develop it. It is the sort of formula that looks rigorous right up until you try to put a number into it, which is more or less the point. Complexity grows exponentially with the number of insights you need to solve a problem. Most problem solving is the work between these insights. You have a eureka moment, then spend months developing the hint until another conceptual jump becomes possible. For an expert, time spent is a useful proxy for this work, hence t. Hand someone the first unit-distance hint and they still have to do enough work to reach the generalized construction. Useful, but post hoc. You can’t look at the problem and predict it would need x number of hints. So, a problem’s age, the number of tries, and the prize attached to it are common proxies to ascribe difficulty. rss.title: Securing our frontier model training environment
rss.summary: OpenAI explains how we strengthened containment for frontier model training and evaluation, including offline environments and high-compute red-teaming.
rss.text_excerpt:
This post describes how we secure the environments that we use to train and evaluate frontier models. These research settings differ from those in which customers use our released models: models in development may not yet have completed safety and alignment training, and we deliberately test them under adversarial conditions to expose weaknesses. Before making models available for broader use, we conduct safety and alignment assessments and put production safeguards in place. In order to work with software, AI models need computing environments: digital workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and attempt different approaches to solving problems. These environments allow models to practice these skills, while also restricting what they can access or do—helping contain the consequences when models make mistakes or exhibit misaligned behavior. But as models become more capable, they become better at finding ways around those limits. A sophisticated model might exploit a software flaw or misconfiguration to escape a sandbox, exploit an internal service to reach the live internet, or find unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes. The Hugging Face incident in July, as well as other examples of model misalignment ⁠ (opens in a new window) that we’ve observed, demonstrates how models with sophisticated cyber capabilities can bypass containment during their training and evaluation. In response to those incidents, we’ve substantially hardened the security of our research environments. Working closely with cloud providers, we’ve added new controls throughout our infrastructure, reduced the attack surface that agents can exploit, and improved our methods for detecting misaligned behavior and attempts to cross security boundaries. These protections overlap, so that containment can hold even if an individual control fails—a strategy known as defense in depth . Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access. We’ve implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access. rss.title: OpenAI and Poland’s NASK partner to advance AI safety and security
rss.summary: OpenAI and Poland’s NASK are partnering on AI safety, security, and technical research to strengthen safeguards and support a more resilient digital ecosystem.
rss.text_excerpt:
OpenAI and Poland’s NASK National Research Institute have signed an agreement to explore collaboration on AI safety, security and technical research. The partnership will bring together expertise from both organizations to better understand emerging risks, strengthen safeguards, and explore how advanced AI can contribute to a more secure and resilient digital ecosystem. As AI systems become more capable, international collaboration between developers and public research institutions will be essential to understanding their risks and building stronger safeguards. OpenAI’s existing work with the US Center for Advancing Standards and Innovation for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), UK AI Security Institute (AISI) and other public research institutions around the world has already helped strengthen safeguards, identify and fix security vulnerabilities in AI agents, and advance frontier AI safety. Through the agreement, NASK’s AI Safety Research Center – serving as the Polish Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (AISI) – and OpenAI will collaborate on AI safety research, exploring ways to evaluate increasingly capable AI systems, identify potential vulnerabilities and strengthen safeguards. OpenAI has called for the US to work with countries around the world on international technical standards for frontier AI, drawing on the expertise of AI safety institutes and standards bodies. Common approaches to evaluating capabilities, assessing risks, testing safeguards and reporting incidents can help countries compare evidence and respond to risks that cross borders. The collaboration with NASK reflects the value of bringing national expertise into this wider effort. In NASK’s case, this expertise rests on extensive research in AI safety, applied directly to protecting public services and Poland’s digital information ecosystem. Without national partners like NASK, global AI safety standards may remain detached from the realities in which AI is actually used. At scale, their latency and cost add up. Today, we’re making the Decisions API generally available. Built with GPT‑6 Luna , the Decisions API focuses Luna’s intelligence on questions with bounded answers, helping applications and agents make near real-time decisions from text, images, and structured inputs up to 10x faster than GPT‑6 Luna through the Responses API. Developers can also pass native JSON inputs, include images in question instructions, and ask up to 400 questions per request, twice the previous limit. We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. When Codex came out, someone on the team asked me, “What do we do when Codex can just one-shot the use cases we spent the last few months building?” That question gets to the heart of what FDE means at OpenAI. > [r.uby.dev](https://r.uby.dev/llm) project. Welcome to the canonical llm.rb repository. llm.rb is a runtime for building agentic AI applications on CRuby. It has zero runtime dependencies by default, supports concurrent and parallel tool execution and has a single coherent API that spans 15+ providers. The README covers a lot of ground and the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md) tracks what has changed between releases. ## Install ##### v17 The v17 series requires Ruby 3.4 or later.
```bash gem install llm.rb ``` ##### v18 The v18 series is available as a prerelease.
It requires Ruby 4.0.0 or later. Ruby 4.1.0+ is recommended. ```bash gem install llm.rb --pre ``` ## Quick start ### Agents The [`LLM::Agent`](https://r.uby.dev/api-docs/llm.rb/LLM/Agent.html) class is the default high-level interface, and it is recommended for most use-cases. It manages the tool loop and provides configurable features on top of it. For example you can manage the tool loop with a retry budget and a tool call budget - alongside other features. The runtime is designed to keep the tool loop alive and it will rescue exceptions. When an exception is encountered in a tool it is reported back to the model as an in-band error that allows the model to change course or retry with different parameters. A tool call requires a tool return (or response), and the lack of one can corrupt the conversation and lead to API-level errors from a provider. But sometimes it is unavoidable (for example, via an interrupt or power loss) so the runtime automatically closes tool calls that fall into that category by telling the model the tool call(s) were cancelled. ##### helloworld.rb A classic "hello world" example.

Our team runs Claude Duet on our own accounts and we use it for work every day. In 2025 we published our framework for safe and trustworthy agents (opens in new tab) , which puts people in control and treats privacy and secure interactions as basic requirements. In July 2026, AISI identified an incident during our cybersecurity evaluations in which models took unsanctioned actions against real people not involved in the evaluation. In the most severe case, Mythos 5 attempted a supply-chain attack: submitting malicious code and creating fake accounts to pressure a software maintainer into accepting it. Although no real-world harm was caused, this was still a serious incident worth understanding and responding to thoroughly. As a first step in understanding the incident’s underlying contributing causes, we published an incident report outlining what happened and the immediate steps we were taking in response. Since then, we have undertaken extensive work to improve evaluation security, sandboxing and monitoring, outlined in our recent blog . These protections are essential: evaluation environments must prevent models from causing harm regardless of whether they behave as expected. Alongside this work, we have investigated an additional dimension of what happened: how failures of model alignment (whether an AI model reliably acts as intended, including respecting the limits it has been given) contributed to the incident, and what we can learn from them. This matters beyond AI evaluation: as models are increasingly used to carry out long tasks without human supervision, it is important to understand if, when, why, and how they take unintended or unexpected actions. Anthropic have independently performed their own alignment analysis of the incident. Today, we are publishing a detailed technical report outlining our results. aihot.summary: Anthropic 发布对 Claude Mythos 5 对齐问题的评估报告。
aihot.text_excerpt:
On August 4, 2026, the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) published a report that detailed some concerning behavior it observed from Claude Mythos 5 during its testing of the model’s cyber capabilities. In AISI’s evaluation, Mythos 5 was given a capture-the-flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenge, in which it was asked to retrieve a protected piece of data (the “flag”) from a simulated network. Internet access was deliberately enabled (this was standard for AISI’s cyber testing at the time, but is no longer). The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations. In this post, which is being published alongside an independent report from AISI, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment. Like AISI’s report, we concentrate on the transcript (the complete record of the model’s reasoning and actions) from a single evaluation run. In this run: To capture the flag, Claude Mythos 5 was tasked with breaking into a small network of computers that AISI had built for the test, designed to resemble a real organization’s systems. It attempted—unsuccessfully—a range of approaches that targeted these systems using the methods that the evaluation intended. However, it also quickly found evidence that one of these machines periodically contacted GitHub, which hosts code repositories. After its initial, within-bounds attempts failed, Mythos 5 searched GitHub for a repository that it believed one of the machines downloaded software from automatically. This repository, however, actually belonged to unrelated human developers. Mythos 5 attempted to submit malicious code to the repository, reasoning that doing so would infect the CTF's machine when it next downloaded the code, and, therefore, could compromise the machine. The model then created fake user identities that contacted the maintainer of the repository in an attempt to pressure them into approving the code change.
